materials.title: At lunch
materials.text:
Choose the best reply in each short conversation.

Dad: ____

2. Child: Can I have some water, please?
Dad: ____

3. Dad: Do you want an apple or a banana?
Child: ____

4. Dad: Is this your lunch box?
Child: ____

5. Child: This soup is hot!
Dad: ____

questions.prompt:
Child: I'm hungry.
Dad: ____
questions.explanation: Hunger is naturally answered by offering lunch. A bus, a person's identity and a book's colour do not address hunger.

questions.prompt:
Child: Can I have some water, please?
Dad: ____
questions.explanation: Yes. Here you are grants the water request. Age, bag ownership and a man's height are unrelated replies.

questions.prompt:
Dad: Do you want an apple or a banana?
Child: ____
questions.explanation: A banana selects one of the two offered foods. Location, name and bedtime farewell do not choose a fruit.

questions.prompt:
Dad: Is this your lunch box?
Child: ____
questions.explanation: Yes, it's mine confirms ownership of the lunch box. Ability, weekday and another child's age do not answer the ownership question.

questions.prompt:
Child: This soup is hot!
Dad: ____
options: Wait a little, then eat it.
questions.explanation: Waiting before eating responds to soup being too hot. Shoes, the cat's size and a location do not address the immediate food-temperature concern.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 自行车检查与新路线
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages with four questions each form this practice. The source records a larger reading section; this is an explicitly declared complete-passage practice selection, not a reproduction of its full section.

materials.title: A. Saturday bicycle check
materials.text:
The school bicycle club will hold a bicycle check on Saturday morning, from 9:00 to 11:30. Bring your bicycle to the covered area behind the sports hall. Please do not leave it at the main door, because another club needs that entrance.

Club members will help you check your tyres, brakes and lights. They can show you how to add air to a tyre, but they cannot replace broken parts. If your bicycle needs new parts, they will give you a note to take to a repair shop. You do not need to buy anything at the event.

Students under twelve must come with an adult. Each check takes about fifteen minutes. There is no booking system, so please join the line when you arrive. The last new check will begin at 11:15.

Bring your own helmet if you would like advice about how it fits. The club has no helmets for sale or loan. Heavy rain will not cancel the event because the area has a roof. However, strong winds may make it unsafe; check the school website after 8:00 before setting off.

questions.prompt: Where should visitors take their bicycles?
options: To the covered area behind the sports hall.
Inside the repair shop beside the school.
questions.explanation: The notice explicitly gives the covered area behind the sports hall. The main entrance is reserved; no on-site repair-shop or library location is given.

questions.prompt: What can club members do at the event?
options: Teach visitors how to add air to a tyre.
Lend a bicycle to every visitor.
questions.explanation: Adding air is a skill members can demonstrate. They cannot replace parts; helmets are neither sold nor lent, and bicycle loans are not offered.

questions.prompt: What must an eleven-year-old student do?
questions.explanation: Under-twelves must attend with an adult. There is no booking, no purchase requirement and no checks after the event ends.

questions.prompt: Why should visitors check the website before leaving?
options: To find out which helmet to buy.
To see whether strong winds affect the event.
questions.explanation: Strong winds may make the covered event unsafe, with updates after 8:00. The website is not described as a shop-selection, parts-order or helmet-buying service.

materials.title: B. A longer way to school
materials.text:
For two years, Ravi walked to school along Market Road. It was the shortest route, but every morning he had to wait at three busy crossings. When roadworks closed part of the road, his neighbour suggested a path beside the river.

Ravi thought the new route would take much longer. On the first day, he left home ten minutes early. The riverside path was longer, but it had only one crossing. He reached school five minutes earlier than usual.

The next day, Ravi took a small notebook. He wrote down when he left home and when he arrived. He did this for a week, including one wet morning. The new walk usually took twenty minutes, compared with twenty-five on Market Road. On the wet day, however, the river path was muddy, and he needed thirty minutes.

After the roadworks ended, Ravi did not always choose the same route. On dry days, he enjoyed the river path. After heavy rain, he used Market Road, where the pavement stayed firm.

His neighbour asked if he had found the best way to school. 'I've found two useful ways,' Ravi replied. 'Now I look out of the window before I choose.' A route could be longer on the map but quicker to walk, and the weather could change that again.

questions.prompt: Why did Ravi first try the river path?
options: He had moved to a new home.
He was training for a race.
Part of his usual road was closed.
His school had changed its opening time.
questions.explanation: Roadworks closed part of Market Road. A new home, race and altered school schedule are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: What helped the longer route be quicker on dry days?
options: It was closer to Ravi's house on the map.
A bus carried Ravi along the river.
His neighbour drove him to school.
questions.explanation: The river path has one crossing compared with three busy ones. It is explicitly longer, and Ravi walks rather than taking a bus or car.

questions.prompt: How long did the river walk take on the wet morning?
questions.explanation: The muddy wet-day walk took thirty minutes. Twenty is its usual duration; twenty-five belongs to Market Road; ten is the extra early departure on day one.

questions.prompt: How did Ravi choose his route after the roadworks?
options: He always took the shortest one on the map.
He considered the weather and path conditions.
He followed whichever neighbour left first.
He avoided walking to school altogether.
questions.explanation: He uses the river path when dry and firm Market Road after rain. A ignores weather; C invents following neighbours; D contradicts his continued walking.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 种子日记与书中便条
units.alignmentNote: Two whole original passages, four questions each, selected as a practice from the recorded larger reading-section task. Not a claim that the source section itself has only eight questions.

materials.title: A. Two seed pots
materials.text:
Sofia planted two bean seeds for a school project. She put each one in a pot with the same kind of soil. Both pots stood beside the kitchen window, and she gave them the same amount of water. She labelled them A and B.

After four days, a green shoot appeared in Pot A. Nothing showed in Pot B. Sofia wanted to dig up B to see what had happened, but her brother suggested waiting. 'You may hurt it if it has already started growing under the soil,' he said.

Instead, Sofia recorded what she could see. Each morning she drew the pots and measured the shoot in A. Three days later, a shoot appeared in B too. It was smaller, but it looked healthy.

At school, Sofia's friend asked which seed was better. Sofia looked at her diary. 'A appeared first,' she said. 'But I don't know yet which plant will grow taller.'

She continued the diary for another two weeks. Sometimes A grew faster; sometimes B did. Her teacher liked the dates beside the drawings. Without them, the pictures would have shown two plants, but not how their growth had changed over time.

questions.prompt: What was the same for the two pots?
options: The size of their shoots after four days.
The day their shoots first appeared.
The name written on each label.
The amount of water Sofia gave them.
questions.explanation: She watered both equally. Shoots appeared on different days and had different sizes; labels A and B differed.

questions.prompt: Why did Sofia's brother suggest waiting?
options: The school project had already ended.
Digging might damage growth below the soil.
He wanted to replace both seeds with flowers.
The soil was too hard for any plant to grow.
questions.explanation: He warns she could hurt a seed already growing below the surface. The project continues; replacement and impossible soil are not stated.

questions.prompt: When did a shoot appear in Pot B?
options: Three days after the shoot in A.
Four days before the shoot in A.
Two weeks before the project started.
On the same morning as the shoot in A.
questions.explanation: Three days after A's appearance, B produced a shoot. The other timings contradict the sequence.

questions.prompt: Why were the dates useful in Sofia's diary?
options: They proved A would always be taller.
They replaced the need to observe the plants.
They connected the drawings with changes over time.
They showed where Sofia bought the seeds.
questions.explanation: Dates reveal when each growth stage occurred. They do not prove a permanent winner, replace observations or identify a seller.

materials.title: B. A note in a library book
materials.text:
When Owen borrowed a mystery story, a small piece of paper fell from between its pages. On it someone had written, 'Check the train time on page 64.' Owen wondered whether the note would give away the ending. He put it aside and started reading.

Halfway through the book, a detective asked how a visitor could be in two towns on the same evening. Owen remembered the note. He looked at page 64 and found a station timetable mentioned in a conversation. It helped him understand an important clue, but it did not tell him who had committed the crime.

When Owen returned the book, he showed the paper to the librarian. She explained that a reading group had discussed the story the previous month. One member sometimes wrote notes to remember questions for the meeting. The paper had probably been left behind by accident.

'Can I add my own note for the next reader?' Owen asked. The librarian smiled but gave him a different idea. The library had a review board where readers could leave comments without putting paper inside books. Owen wrote, 'Watch the small details. One ordinary conversation may matter later.' He did not mention the page number. He wanted the next reader to enjoy finding the clue too.

questions.prompt: Why did Owen put the note aside at first?
options: He thought it belonged to a train driver.
He did not want it to reveal the story's ending.
He could not read the handwriting.
questions.explanation: He feared the note might give away the ending and began without it. Its author is not a driver; unreadable handwriting and prior reading are not stated.

questions.prompt: What did Owen find on page 64?
options: The name of the criminal printed alone.
A list of all the reading-group members.
A timetable mentioned in a conversation.
questions.explanation: The station timetable provides a clue. It does not explicitly reveal the criminal, list members or explain library membership.

questions.prompt: What did the librarian think had happened to the note?
options: A reading-group member had left it accidentally.
The author had printed it inside every copy.
A child had hidden a train ticket in the book.
Owen had written it during his last visit.
questions.explanation: A member likely left a meeting reminder behind. It was loose handwritten paper, not a printed feature or train ticket, and Owen found rather than authored it.

questions.prompt: Why did Owen leave out the page number in his review?
options: The board did not allow any numbers.
He could no longer remember it.
He wanted readers to avoid the book.
He wanted others to discover the clue themselves.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states his wish that the next reader enjoy discovery. No numerical ban, memory failure or wish to discourage readers is described.
